Chapter 8

Road Traffic Act 1994

The legal framework behind Dutch driving: alcohol and drugs, driving licences, enforcement, medical fitness and beginner-driver rules.

  • Alcohol & Drugs
  • Driving Licences
  • Enforcement & Sanctions
  • Fitness to Drive
  • Beginner Drivers

The Wegenverkeerswet 1994 (WVW 1994) is the main Dutch road-traffic statute. The RVV 1990 is one of the regulations made under that statutory framework and contains many of the day-to-day rules of the road.

This chapter also refers to related rules that sit outside the WVW itself — including the Reglement rijbewijzen, the Regeling eisen geschiktheid 2000, the WAHV administrative-enforcement system and CBR measures. That distinction matters: not every licence, medical or fine rule is written directly in the WVW 1994.

Alcohol & Drugs

Article 8 WVW 1994 sets the core prohibition on driving under the influence; different limits apply to experienced and beginner drivers.

Experienced Drivers 0.5 ‰ / 220 µg/l

For an experienced driver, the statutory alcohol limit is 0.5 ‰ alcohol in the blood, corresponding to 220 micrograms per litre of exhaled breath. Driving above that limit is prohibited.

The limit is a legal threshold, not a safety target. Alcohol can impair judgement and reaction time before the legal limit is reached.

Beginner Drivers 0.2 ‰ / 88 µg/l

A beginner driver is subject to the lower limit of 0.2 ‰ in blood or 88 micrograms per litre of exhaled breath. The beginner period is not always five years: depending on the age and first licence category, it lasts five or seven years.

Being a professional driver does not by itself create a separate 0.2 ‰ alcohol limit. The lower statutory limit is tied to beginner-driver status.

Drugs: Statutory Thresholds, Not One Universal “Zero” Rule Article 8

Dutch law sets statutory blood-concentration limits for specified drugs including cannabis (THC), cocaine, amphetamine-type substances, heroin/morphine and GHB. For single-substance use, each listed substance has its own threshold.

When drugs are combined with other drugs, alcohol or certain other impairing substances, substantially lower combination limits apply. Government guidance describes this combination-use approach as a zero-limit policy. Driving can also be prohibited under the general impairment rule even where a substance is not one of the specifically listed drugs.

Medicines Can Also Affect Driving Check before driving

Some prescribed medicines contain substances that are also covered by the statutory drug limits, such as medicinal cannabis, dexamphetamine or morphine. Other medicines may still make driving unsafe because of drowsiness, slowed reactions or impaired concentration.

Follow the medicine instructions and discuss driving with a doctor or pharmacist when necessary. A prescription does not create a general exemption from the rules on impaired driving.

Criminal Case and CBR Measure Are Separate

Drink- or drug-driving can lead to a criminal case and can also trigger a separate CBR administrative measure. Depending on the alcohol level and circumstances, the CBR may impose a light alcohol course (LEMA), an EMA course, or an investigation into fitness to drive. These are not the same as the fine, prosecution or driving disqualification imposed through the criminal-law process.

Driving Licences

The Dutch licence categories follow the European system, but age, trailer and professional-driver rules require careful reading.

Who Does What? CBR · RDW · Municipality

The CBR conducts driving examinations and assesses driving fitness. After you pass, the licence document is applied for and issued through the municipality; the RDW maintains the central driving-licence register and records the relevant declarations and licence data.

So it is inaccurate to say that the CBR itself “issues” the Dutch driving licence.

Category B and Trailers

With category B, a trailer with a permitted maximum mass of up to 750 kg may be towed. A trailer over 750 kg is also possible if the permitted maximum mass of the car and trailer together does not exceed 3,500 kg. Category B+ (code 96) extends the combination limit to 4,250 kg. Heavier combinations can require BE.

2toDrive — What Actually Happens at 17

A young person may take the category B practical test from age 17. After passing, they apply for the real driving licence; they do not wait until 18 for another “standard” test. Until age 18 they may drive only in the Netherlands with an approved coach and the required accompanying-driver pass. A coach is normally at least 27 years old and has held a valid B licence for at least five years.

Licence Validity Current validity rules

As a general maximum, categories AM, A1, A2, A, B, BE and T are valid for up to 10 years. The heavy categories C1, C1E, C, CE, D1, D1E, D and DE are valid for up to 5 years.

  • Age 65–69 at renewal: the new licence normally runs until the 75th birthday.
  • Age 70–74: the licence is normally valid for a maximum of 5 years.
  • Expiry on or after age 75: medical assessment is required for renewal; the renewed licence is generally valid for a maximum of 5 years unless the CBR sets a shorter period.
  • Heavy C/D categories: medical assessment is required at each renewal.

Medical restrictions can result in a shorter validity period.

Enforcement & Sanctions

Administrative fines, criminal proceedings and CBR measures are different legal tracks.

WAHV Administrative Fines Mulder fines

Many common traffic violations are handled under the WAHV (Wet administratiefrechtelijke handhaving verkeersvoorschriften). Examples include many speeding offences, red-light violations, parking violations and other fact-coded traffic offences.

A WAHV sanction is an administrative fine. There is a statutory procedure for challenging the decision; it should not be described as if there were no route of review.

Speeding

Sanction and procedure depend on the amount by which the limit is exceeded and on the vehicle type. Very large excess speeds can move outside ordinary administrative handling and can trigger licence-surrender rules.

Red traffic light

Passing a red light is a common enforceable traffic offence and can be detected by police or automated enforcement.

Handheld electronic device

Holding a mobile electronic device while driving is prohibited. Separate rules and sanction amounts apply to different road-user categories.

Seatbelts and children

For a child under 12, the driver is responsible for compliance with the restraint rules. Older passengers can receive the fine themselves if they fail to use the required seatbelt.

Parking

Illegal parking can lead to a fine. In some local situations a vehicle can also be removed under separate municipal powers and procedures.

Criminal offences

Drink- and drug-driving, dangerous driving, hit-and-run and other serious conduct can be handled under criminal law. Possible consequences include a fine, community service or imprisonment and disqualification from driving, depending on the offence and circumstances.

Licence Surrender and Confiscation Article 164 WVW

For specified serious cases, police require the driver to surrender the licence immediately. Important examples include:

  • Alcohol: more than 1.3 ‰ for an experienced driver, or more than 0.8 ‰ for a beginner driver.
  • Speed: 50 km/h or more above the applicable limit for a motor vehicle, or 30 km/h or more for a moped, where the statutory conditions are met.
  • Refusal: refusal to cooperate with the required alcohol investigation.
  • Serious danger: conduct that seriously endangers road safety can also lead to immediate action.

After police surrender/confiscation, the licence goes to the public prosecutor, who decides within the statutory period whether it will be retained or returned. A CBR procedure can run separately, but the CBR does not automatically decide every Article 164 confiscation.

Three Different Questions

WAHV: is an administrative fine due? Criminal law: is the driver prosecuted and punished? CBR: does road safety require a course, investigation, suspension or invalidation based on driving skill or fitness? One incident can sometimes lead to more than one of these processes.

Fitness to Drive

The CBR assesses medical fitness in specified situations; the current system does not impose a blanket reporting duty for every new medical condition.

When a Health Declaration Is Used CBR assessment

A Health Declaration (Gezondheidsverklaring) is used in several situations, including when taking a driving examination (except category AM), when renewing a licence that has limited medical validity, when applying for or renewing heavy C/D categories, and when renewing at age 75 or older where the age-related medical procedure applies.

The CBR may request additional medical information, an examination by a doctor or specialist, or a driving test before deciding whether the person is fit to drive and for how long.

Group 1 Vision Standards A / B / BE and similar

For Group 1 licences, the general visual standards include:

  • Visual acuity: binocular visual acuity of at least 0.5, with correction if necessary.
  • Visual field: at least 120° horizontally, extending at least 50° to both left and right and 20° upward and downward, with no visual-field defect within the central 20°.
  • Colour vision: no separate colour-vision requirement.

Special or exceptional cases can be subject to additional ophthalmological assessment and, in some cases, a CBR driving test.

If Your Health Changes Do not overstate the reporting rule

As of 2026, there is no general statutory duty requiring every licence holder to report every newly developed medical condition to the CBR. Government guidance says that if your health changes and you are unsure about driving, you should discuss the effect on driving fitness with your doctor; you may submit a Health Declaration so the CBR can assess you.

This does not mean you may drive when your condition or medication makes safe driving impossible. General road-safety duties and the rules on impairment continue to apply.

Fatigue Has No Separate Promille-Style Limit

Dutch law does not set a numerical “fatigue limit” comparable to an alcohol limit. Severe fatigue can nevertheless lead to unsafe or dangerous driving and can therefore have legal consequences under the general road-safety rules. Treat fatigue as a safety issue, not as a separate intoxication category.

The Beginner-Driver Period

The Dutch beginnersrijbewijs is an ordinary licence with additional rules for new drivers; the period can be five or seven years.

Five or Seven Years Beginnersrijbewijs

Everyone who obtains a first driving licence becomes a beginner driver, regardless of age or licence category. The duration depends on when and which first licence was obtained:

  • First licence at age 16: generally 7 years.
  • Category B obtained at age 17: 5 years.
  • First licence at age 18 or older: 5 years.
  • AM as the first licence: special timing rules can produce a 7-year beginner period; obtaining B at 17 can change the period to 5 years.

The lower 0.2 ‰ alcohol limit applies while the driver has beginner status.

Penalty Points for Serious Offences Beginner system

The beginnersrijbewijs includes a penalty-point system for specified serious traffic offences. Examples can include serious speeding, tailgating or causing an accident when the statutory conditions for a point are met.

After a second registered serious offence and therefore a second beginner point, the Public Prosecution Service reports the driver to the CBR. The CBR then investigates driving skill and can take a measure. This is different from saying that every beginner offence automatically causes a retest.

CBR Alcohol Measures LEMA · EMA · Investigation

The CBR alcohol-measure thresholds are separate from the basic criminal alcohol limit. Under the current rules, important ranges include:

  • LEMA: generally 0.8–<1.0 ‰ for an experienced driver, and 0.5–<0.8 ‰ for a beginner driver.
  • EMA: generally 1.0–<1.8 ‰ for an experienced driver, and 0.8–<1.3 ‰ for a beginner driver.
  • Fitness investigation: generally from 1.8 ‰ for an experienced driver and from 1.3 ‰ for a beginner driver.

Repeat incidents, refusal to cooperate, accidents and other statutory circumstances can change which CBR measure applies. These thresholds should therefore be learned as part of the CBR administrative system, not as the basic legal alcohol limit itself.

Experienced driver
  • Alcohol limit: 0.5 ‰
  • Article 164 alcohol surrender threshold: above 1.3 ‰
  • Not subject to the beginner penalty-point system
  • Still subject to the separate alcohol recidivism points system that applies to all drivers
Beginner driver
  • Alcohol limit: 0.2 ‰
  • Article 164 alcohol surrender threshold: above 0.8 ‰
  • Additional penalty-point system for specified serious offences
  • Beginner status lasts 5 or 7 years, depending on the first licence and age
Chapter 8 — What to Take Away

Article 8 WVW: the alcohol limit is 0.5 ‰ for experienced drivers and 0.2 ‰ for beginner drivers; professional status alone does not create the lower limit. Drugs are governed by statutory thresholds, with stricter combination-use limits.

Licences: the CBR examines and assesses fitness, the municipality issues the licence document and the RDW maintains the register. Category and validity rules vary by vehicle, age and medical status.

Enforcement: WAHV fines, criminal proceedings, police licence confiscation and CBR measures are distinct legal mechanisms. Fitness: the CBR uses the Health Declaration in defined situations, and there is no blanket statutory duty to report every new medical condition. Beginner drivers: the period can last five or seven years and includes a separate serious-offence points system.
